title: Always on the Search for Talent
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece profiles a habit shared by great leaders: they never stop scouting for talent, even outside formal hiring cycles. Encountering exceptional service or skill anywhere — a restaurant, a vendor interaction — prompts these leaders to open a door for a future conversation rather than let the moment pass. The article is careful to distinguish this behavior from poaching competitors' staff, framing it instead as attentiveness paired with respect. It also connects this instinct to a leader's involvement in their own organization's formal recruiting, arguing that leaders who stay hands-on in interviewing, even for junior roles, send an organization-wide signal about how much people matter.
points: Great leaders treat talent-spotting as a continuous, informal practice rather than something confined to open requisitions.
The habit is distinguished from poaching — it is described as leaving a conversational door open, not making unsolicited job offers to competitors' staff.
Leaders who personally engage in recruiting, even for the most junior hires, send an organization-wide message about the priority placed on people.
The piece frames unearthing new talent as one of the most satisfying parts of leadership, tying personal curiosity about people to organizational success.
quotes: More importantly, they are always on the search for talent, no matter where it might be.
Good leaders are respectful about engaging talent linked to competitors or affiliated organizations.
By establishing a conversation with special people, they leave the door open for possibilities in the future.
They don’t wait for open positions and official searches to begin looking for talent.
When the busiest and most experienced leaders commit their time and energy in every aspect of the recruiting process, it sends a loud and important message to the larger organization.
Perhaps nothing satisfies a great leader more than unearthing new talent.
